summary: Specifies the syntax of two URI schemes for the TURN protocol, used to provision the TURN resolution mechanism of RFC 5928. This makes TURN relay servers easy to name in configuration.

eli5.summary: It sets how to write the address of a relay helper, so apps know which one to use.

questions: how to specify a turn server
what is the default turn port
subtitle: Two URI schemes, turn: and turns:, for naming a TURN relay server in a consistent way.

tldr.problem: Applications such as WebRTC need to be told which TURN relay server to use, and an inconsistent way of writing that information leads to ambiguity and non-interoperable solutions.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines the turn and turns URI schemes, which carry a host, an optional port and an optional transport, plus a secure flag implied by the scheme, ready for the TURN resolution mechanism of RFC 5928.
tldr.outcome: A TURN server can be described, configured and exchanged in one standard form, and both schemes are registered as permanent.

today: RFC 7065 is a Proposed Standard. No later RFC is recorded as obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why TURN Needs URIs
sections.content:
TURN lets hosts behind a NAT control a relay server, which exchanges packets with their peers. The peers may be behind NATs too. The protocol itself is defined in RFC 5766.

With standards such as WebRTC, the RFC expects many endpoints and web applications to need to identify a TURN server. They must be provisioned with the right configuration, and inconsistent syntax adds ambiguity and can cause non-interoperable solutions. The turn and turns URI schemes give a consistent way to describe, configure and exchange this information.

RFC 5928 defines a resolution mechanism that turns a secure flag, a host name or IP address, a possibly empty port and a possibly empty transport into a list of address, port and transport tuples. The new URIs carry exactly those four components.
sections.eli5: A helper computer needs an address everyone writes the same way. Otherwise one app writes it one way, another app a different way, and they cannot understand each other.

sections.title: URI Syntax
sections.content:
The formal ABNF is: a scheme of turn or turns, a colon, a host, an optional colon and port, and an optional ?transport= followed by udp, tcp or an extension made of one or more unreserved characters. The host and port productions come from RFC 3986.

That does not make these hierarchical URIs. Developers MUST NOT use a generic hierarchical URI parser on a turn or turns URI.

The host, port and transport are passed unchanged to the RFC 5928 algorithm. The secure flag is false for turn and true for turns.
sections.eli5: The address has a few fixed slots: which door type, which house, which room number and how to deliver. You fill in what you know and skip the rest.

sections.title: Meaning of the Schemes
sections.content:
Both schemes designate a TURN server, also called a relay. TURN can run over UDP, TCP or TLS-over-TCP. The turns scheme MUST be used when TURN runs over TLS-over-TCP (or, in the future, DTLS-over-UDP), and turn MUST be used otherwise.

The host is required and names the server. If the port is absent, the default is 3478 for both UDP and TCP, and 5349 for TURN over TLS.
sections.eli5: turns is the version with a lock on the door. If you do not say which door number, there are standard ones to try.

sections.title: Examples
sections.content: The appendix shows how URIs map to the secure flag, port and transport, with example.org as the host. For instance, turn:example.org gives secure false and nothing else, turns:example.org gives secure true, and turn:example.org:8000 sets port 8000. Adding ?transport=udp or ?transport=tcp to turn: sets UDP or TCP, and turns:example.org?transport=tcp yields secure true with transport TLS.
sections.eli5: A few sample addresses show what each one means, like a cheat sheet next to the envelope.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The schemes add no specific security issues beyond those in RFC 3986. The resolution mechanism's security considerations are in Section 5 of RFC 5928, which contains normative text on how clients authenticate when TLS is used.

A turns URI does not carry the username or password. In environments such as WebRTC, those are likely sent by an external agent along with the URI. If they arrived in the clear, using turns would bring little or no benefit, so a TURN client MUST make sure the username, password, turns URI and any other security-relevant parameters are received with equivalent security. Another TLS session can do this if both sessions are similarly parameterised, for example with commensurate strength ciphersuites.
sections.eli5: A locked door does not help if you shout the key across the street. The key has to travel as safely as the address.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC registers both turn and turns as permanent URI schemes, following RFC 4395. The turn scheme is for applications that need to identify a TURN server for NAT traversal, and turns is the same over a secure connection. The change controller is the IESG.
sections.eli5: Both names were written into the official list of address types, so nobody else can use them for something different.

sections.title: Design Notes
sections.content:
The authors record several choices. They kept the s suffix rather than a parameter such as ;proto=tls, to keep symmetry with the STUN URI. Following RFC 4395, and because the URI is not hierarchical, these are opaque URIs.

No password appears in the URI because it is deprecated in RFC 3986, and no username or auth because they do not guide resolution. No generic parameters exist, to prevent compatibility issues.
sections.eli5: The authors explain why they kept the address simple: only the parts that help find the helper are in it.
